questions.subtopic: 2C1 Supervising the engagement. Closer review for an expert in a new, complex area
questions.question: An engagement supervisor plans light review for a senior internal auditor with 12 years of payroll audits and recent derivatives training, on a bank's complex derivative-valuation engagement. What is the supervisor's best course?

options.A: Keep the light review, since the auditor's experience sets how close it is.
options.B: Bring in a valuation specialist to redo the auditor's tests.
options.C: Review the auditor's valuation work closely from planning to sign-off.
options.D: Keep the light review, adding a checklist sign-off on each workpaper.

questions.key_concept: Supervision depth follows the function's maturity, the auditor's experience and the work's complexity together; years in another area do not cover a new, complex one.
questions.pre_read: Supervision depth turns on more than one factor. Which of them does this stem change, and which does it leave alone?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance ties the extent of supervision to the function's maturity, the auditor's proficiency and experience, and the engagement's complexity. The auditor's experience is in payroll, with only training in valuations, and the engagement is complex, so closer review fits. Keeping light review, the runner-up, counts years in another area as experience in this one and passes over complexity.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: experience is one factor in the extent of supervision, but the auditor's is in payroll, and Standard 12.3 also weighs the engagement's complexity, which is high here.
wrong_explanations.B: A specialist fills a competency the team lacks. The auditor has the training, so the need is closer supervision of the work, not a second party redoing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 12.3's considerations offer checklists where no supervisor is available. Here a supervisor is, and complexity calls for closer review; a checklist on light review does not supply it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the auditor has the training, so redoing the tests answers a competency gap that is not there, and D, because a checklist supports oversight; it does not deepen light review.
Final two: C beats A because experience counts in the area being audited, and complexity also sets the extent of supervision; here both point to closer review.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about how closely to supervise, check all three factors: the function's maturity, the auditor's experience in this area, and the engagement's complexity.

questions.subtopic: 2C1 Supervising the engagement. A conclusion wider than the tests behind it
questions.question: Checking workpapers on a retailer's stock engagement, the engagement supervisor reads an internal auditor's conclusion that all six warehouses reconcile stock monthly; the auditor tested the two nearest. What is the supervisor's best response?

options.A: Sign off, since both tested warehouses reconcile monthly.
options.B: Narrow the draft report's conclusion to the two warehouses tested.
options.C: Have the auditor get written confirmations from the other four managers.
options.D: Raise a review note questioning the conclusion's reach past the tests.

questions.key_concept: A conclusion wider than its evidence goes back through a review note: the auditor widens the tests or narrows the conclusion in the workpapers.
questions.pre_read: What do two warehouses' tests support, and where does a supervisor's doubt get resolved: in the workpapers or in the draft?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance has the supervisor confirm that workpapers support the conclusions, and its considerations let the supervisor ask for more evidence or clarification. Two warehouses picked for nearness do not support a claim about six, so a review note sends it back: the auditor widens the tests or narrows the conclusion, and the workpapers change. Narrowing the draft, the runner-up, leaves the unsupported workpaper behind.

wrong_explanations.A: Passing tests at two warehouses support a conclusion about those two. The supervisor confirms the workpapers support the conclusion as written, and these do not support all six.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the claim must narrow or the evidence widen, but workpapers are the primary support for communications; the review note gets them amended before any draft changes.
wrong_explanations.C: Confirmations from the managers responsible for the warehouses are weaker evidence than tests (Standard 14.1), and they would not show four warehouses' reconciliations work.

tips: Eliminate: A, because two warehouses' results cannot support a conclusion about six, and C, because statements from the managers responsible are weaker evidence than the auditor's own tests.
Final two: D beats B because workpapers are the primary support for any communication; a review note gets them amended, by more tests or a narrower conclusion, before the draft changes.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about a supervisor's review, doubts go back to the auditor through review notes for evidence or clarification; the supervisor does not edit the result alone.

questions.subtopic: 2C1 Supervising the engagement. Rating an auditor whose work was mostly interviews
questions.question: At an insurer, an internal auditor's work was mostly interviews, all attended by the claims manager, most by the engagement supervisor; workpapers record only conclusions. What is the supervisor's best basis for assessing the auditor?

options.A: The workpapers the auditor prepared, the record supervision rests on.
options.B: Direct observation of the auditor's work during the engagement.
options.C: The claims manager's rating, since the manager saw more of the work.
options.D: The auditor's self-assessment, agreed at a meeting after the engagement.

questions.key_concept: Assessing an auditor's skills reaches beyond workpaper review: what the supervisor sees in interviews and meetings during the engagement is part of the evaluation.
questions.pre_read: Where did the auditor's work on this engagement actually happen, and where could a supervisor see it?
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance treat skill assessment as ongoing and wider than workpaper review, and Standard 10.2 requires the chief audit executive to evaluate each auditor's competencies. The auditor's work was mostly interviews, and the workpapers record only conclusions, so what the supervisor saw of them is the best basis. The workpapers, the runner-up, support supervision but cannot show how the auditor conducted interviews.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: workpapers are a basis for supervising auditors (Standard 14.6), but skill assessment reaches beyond them, and they cannot show how the auditor conducted the interviews the supervisor attended.
wrong_explanations.C: The manager saw more, but an evaluation resting mainly on the reviewed area's input may impair objectivity: auditors could soften results to score well (Standard 2.2).
wrong_explanations.D: A self-assessment can feed a development talk, but the supervisor evaluates performance; a rating resting on the auditor's own view gives no independent judgment of the work.

tips: Eliminate: C, because an evaluation resting mainly on the reviewed manager's view may impair objectivity, however much the manager saw, and D, because the supervisor, not the auditor, judges the performance.
Final two: B beats A because skill assessment reaches beyond workpaper review, and the auditor's work happened mostly in interviews, most of which the supervisor attended.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about evaluating auditors, look at the work they actually did, seen throughout the engagement, not at one record or one party's view.

questions.subtopic: 2C1 Supervising the engagement. Supervising a cosourced firm's tests
questions.question: Internal audit at an airline cosources an engagement's IT tests to a certified firm under the approved program; the firm offers its own quality review instead of supervision. What is the engagement supervisor's best response?

options.A: Review the firm's workpapers for support, as for staff work.
options.B: Accept the firm's quality review, as the firm is certified.
options.C: Have the firm adopt the function's methodology for its IT tests.
options.D: Repeat the firm's IT tests with staff before using the results.

questions.key_concept: Engagement work done by an outside service provider is supervised like staff work; the chief audit executive stays responsible, whoever performs it.
questions.pre_read: Are these tests part of internal audit's own engagement, or another provider's separate work? The answer sets the duty.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.3 Oversee and Improve Engagement Performance makes the chief audit executive responsible for supervising engagements whether staff or other service providers do the work; supervision may be delegated, but responsibility stays. So the engagement supervisor reviews the firm's workpapers as for staff. Accepting the firm's own review, the runner-up, fits relying on another assurance provider's separate work under Standard 9.5, not tests done inside this engagement.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 9.5 lets the chief audit executive rely, on a documented basis, on other providers' separate work. These tests sit inside the engagement, so they are supervised.
wrong_explanations.C: Working to the function's methodology helps, but it does not replace supervision: the chief audit executive stays responsible for supervising work that service providers do (Standard 12.3).
wrong_explanations.D: Reperforming suits work whose competence or care is in doubt. Supervision means reviewing the workpapers for support; nothing here suggests the firm's tests need redoing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because working to the function's methodology does not replace supervision of the work, and D, because nothing suggests the tests need redoing; reviewing them is the duty.
Final two: A beats B because work a service provider does inside the engagement is supervised like staff work; relying on another provider's own separate work is a different case.
Exam cue: on CIA questions with outside help, ask whether the work sits inside the engagement (supervise it) or is another provider's separate work (evaluate it and document the reliance).

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. A timing change with the scope unchanged
questions.question: A system freeze pushes an internal auditor's fieldwork in a utility's billing unit two weeks later; objectives, scope, work program and budgeted hours stay unchanged. Which step is the auditor most clearly required to take?

options.A: Get the chief audit executive's approval before changing the dates.
options.B: Ask billing management to agree to the new dates first.
options.C: Tell billing management about the new dates promptly.
options.D: Note the new dates, and tell management at the closing meeting.

questions.key_concept: Every change to an engagement's timing is communicated with management timely; approval is needed for changes to the objectives, scope or work program.
questions.pre_read: List what changed and what stayed the same. Which changes need approval, and which need only to be communicated?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication requires internal auditors to communicate the objectives, scope and timing with management, and to communicate later changes timely. Telling billing management promptly meets it. Approval by the chief audit executive, the runner-up, is required for changes to the objectives and scope (Standard 13.3) and to the work program (Standard 13.6); here only the dates move.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the chief audit executive approves changes to objectives, scope and the work program, but none of those changes here. A timing change must be communicated with management timely.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 13.1 requires the new dates to be communicated with management, not agreed by it. Seeking management's support is sound, but its agreement is not a precondition in assurance work.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the change is sound, but Standard 13.1 requires changes to be communicated timely; the closing meeting comes too late for a schedule management must plan around.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the new dates must be communicated with management, not first agreed by it, and D, because a change held for the closing meeting is not communicated timely.
Final two: C beats A because approval covers changes to objectives, scope and the work program; a change in timing alone must be communicated with management timely.

Exam cue: on CIA questions about a change mid-engagement, ask what changed: objectives, scope or work program need approval; a change to objectives, scope or timing is communicated with management timely.

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. An opening meeting declined, email instead
questions.question: An internal auditor has finished the risk assessment for a winery's export-rebate assurance engagement, but the export manager, traveling for a month, declines meetings and asks for email instead. What is the auditor's best response?

options.A: Delay fieldwork until the export manager can attend a meeting.
options.B: Email the risk results, objectives, scope and timing, and file it.
options.C: Email the objectives, scope and timing; save risk results for the closing.
options.D: Have the chief audit executive treat the refusal as a scope limitation.

questions.key_concept: Objectives, scope and timing must reach management; a meeting is the preferred way to share them with the risk results, not a requirement.
questions.pre_read: Separate what must reach the manager from the way it is preferably delivered. Which of the two does the refusal affect?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication requires the objectives, scope and timing to be communicated with management; its considerations add the risk assessment results, preferably in a meeting, and a record in the workpapers. A meeting is preferred, not required, so a filed email carries what the manager must hear. Delaying fieldwork, the runner-up, treats the preference as a condition and loses a month.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a meeting is the preferred way to share risk results, objectives and scope, but it is not required; an email carries the same content without a month's delay.
wrong_explanations.C: Risk assessment results should be shared once the assessment is done, with the objectives and scope (Standard 13.1); the closing communication is for finalizing engagement results.
wrong_explanations.D: A scope limitation is a condition that stops the planned work, such as refused access. Declining a meeting while answering by email blocks no planned test.

tips: Eliminate: C, because risk results should be shared once the assessment is done, not held for the closing, and D, because declining a meeting blocks no planned work, so it is no scope limitation.
Final two: B beats A because the content must reach management and a meeting is only the preferred way; email meets the requirement where a meeting cannot happen.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, separate what must be communicated from the preferred way to do it: when the preferred form fails, deliver the required content another way and keep a record.

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. Who decides that a matter reaches the board
questions.question: Mid-fieldwork, an internal auditor finds a refinery safety risk that may exceed the board's risk tolerance, and alerts plant management at once. Who is best placed to decide whether the board hears of it?

options.A: The internal auditor, who judges the finding's significance.
options.B: Senior management, which works with the board on escalation.
options.C: The plant manager, who owns the risk and its response.
options.D: The chief audit executive, applying criteria set with the board.

questions.key_concept: The auditor judges significance and raises the facts; the chief audit executive decides what reaches the board, under escalation criteria agreed with the board.
questions.pre_read: Separate two judgments: how significant the finding is, and whether the board hears of it. Who holds each one?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 Board Interaction makes the chief audit executive responsible for giving the board what it needs, and its essential conditions have the board set expectations with the chief audit executive for which issues are escalated, such as significant risks beyond its tolerance. So the chief audit executive decides, applying those criteria. The internal auditor, the runner-up, judges significance under Standard 14.3, then brings the facts up the line.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the internal auditor judges the finding's significance (Standard 14.3), but escalation to the board runs through the chief audit executive, who applies the criteria agreed with the board.
wrong_explanations.B: Senior management helps the board and the chief audit executive shape how matters are escalated, but it does not decide what internal audit takes to the board.
wrong_explanations.C: The plant manager owns the risk and chooses the response. Owning a risk does not include deciding whether internal audit's concerns about it reach the board.

tips: Eliminate: B, because senior management helps shape the escalation process but does not filter internal audit's reports, and C, because owning the risk means choosing the response, not deciding what the board hears.
Final two: D beats A because the auditor judges significance and raises it, but the chief audit executive takes matters to the board under the criteria agreed with it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about reaching the board, the internal auditor raises the facts; the chief audit executive applies the board's escalation criteria and goes to the board.

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. Who hears a finding during fieldwork
questions.question: Auditing a hotel chain's rate controls, an internal auditor finds front-desk staff making unapproved overrides of rules the revenue director owns; the front-desk supervisor offers to agree a fix. What is the auditor's best course?

options.A: Discuss the finding and possible fixes with the revenue director.
options.B: Agree a fix with the front-desk supervisor, then copy the director.
options.C: Raise the finding with the director at the closing meeting.
options.D: Discuss the finding first with the chain's general manager.

questions.key_concept: Findings and possible actions are discussed promptly with the management authorized to change the activity; supervisors below it can confirm facts, not settle the fix.
questions.pre_read: Who owns the rules being broken? Then ask whether the offer, the timing or the rank of the listener changes that.
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 14.4 Recommendations and Action Plans say findings and possible recommendations should be discussed promptly with the managers who have authority to change and oversee the activity. The override rules are the revenue director's, so the auditor discusses them there, though the front-desk supervisor offers to settle it. Agreeing a fix with that supervisor, the runner-up, settles actions with someone who can confirm facts but does not own the rules.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the front-desk supervisor can confirm facts and help find causes, and a copy informs the director, but actions are discussed with the management that owns the rules.
wrong_explanations.C: The closing communication finalizes results; findings should be discussed promptly so management can act, and nothing here justifies waiting until the end.
wrong_explanations.D: The general manager oversees the whole chain, but the director owns the override rules. Findings go first to the management directly authorized to change the activity.

tips: Eliminate: C, because findings are discussed promptly, not held for the closing communication, and D, because the most senior manager is not the one who owns these rules.
Final two: A beats B because findings and actions are discussed with the management that owns the rules; the front-desk supervisor can confirm facts, and a copy does not make the director a party.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about who hears a finding, pick the manager with authority over the activity: not the staff who did the work, and not simply the most senior person.

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. What the engagement notice carries
questions.question: An internal auditor is drafting the first notice that procurement management will receive for a distillery's assurance engagement. Which of the following best suits the notice?

options.A: The risk assessment results and the initial objectives and scope.
options.B: The reason, start date and length, and a request for documents.
options.C: The draft work program, for the procurement head to approve.
options.D: The planned sample items, so procurement can pull the files early.

questions.key_concept: The engagement notice comes first: the reason, start and likely length, plus a request for what the risk assessment needs. Its results come later.
questions.pre_read: Place the notice in time. What exists before the risk assessment, and what can only come after it?
questions.correct_explanation: The considerations to Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication say the advance notice should give the reason for the engagement, its proposed start and approximate length, and request the information needed to assess risks. A first notice therefore comes before the risk assessment, so its results and the initial objectives and scope, the runner-up, come later, preferably at an opening meeting.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: these follow the engagement risk assessment and are shared with management then, preferably in a meeting. The notice comes first and asks for what that assessment needs.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive, not management, approves an assurance engagement's work program (Standard 13.6). Building it with the requester belongs to advisory work.
wrong_explanations.D: No sample exists before the risk assessment and work program; items are chosen as the approved program sets out and requested during fieldwork.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the chief audit executive, not management, approves an assurance work program, and D, because samples are chosen under the approved work program, which does not exist yet.
Final two: B beats A because the notice comes before the risk assessment; its results, the objectives and the scope are shared after it, preferably at an opening meeting.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about engagement communications, place each message in its stage: notice first, then risk results, objectives and scope, then progress, then results.

questions.subtopic: 2C1 Supervising the engagement. Moving a task to another auditor
questions.question: An engagement supervisor, the chief audit executive's delegate for approvals, moves a flower exporter's customs test, unchanged, mid-fieldwork from an internal auditor now on leave to a replacement auditor. What most clearly must happen?

options.A: The replacement auditor reperforms the finished steps before going on.
options.B: The chief audit executive approves the switch before the replacement auditor starts.
options.C: The supervisor names the replacement auditor in the program and approves the change.
options.D: The replacement auditor goes on; with the test unchanged, the program stands as approved.

questions.key_concept: The work program names who performs each task, so moving a task to another auditor changes the program and needs prompt approval.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the work program must contain, then whether this switch changes it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.6 requires the work program to name the internal auditors assigned to each task, and to be approved before use and promptly when it changes. Moving the customs test to the replacement auditor changes that assignment, so the supervisor, as the delegate, names that auditor and approves the change. Carrying on because the test is unchanged, the closest choice, overlooks that who performs each task is part of the program.

wrong_explanations.A: Reperforming finished work is a review choice when that work looks weak, and nothing here suggests it. What this switch changes is the program's assignment.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive may delegate approval, and the supervisor holds it. Waiting for the chief audit executive's own approval adds a step the Standards do not require here.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the test is unchanged, but the program must name who performs each task (Standard 13.6), so moving it to another auditor changes the program and needs prompt approval.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a change of auditor does not call for reperforming sound finished work, and B, because the supervisor already holds the chief audit executive's delegated approval.
Final two: C beats D because the program names who performs each task, so a reassignment changes the program even when the test itself does not.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, any change to the work program, including who is assigned to a task, needs prompt approval from the chief audit executive or the delegate.

questions.subtopic: 2C2 Communicating during the engagement. A request for oral results only
questions.question: At the closing meeting of a hospital's billing engagement, the billing director asks a staff internal auditor to give the results orally, with no written report, fearing lawsuits. What is the auditor's best response?

options.A: Ask legal counsel whether the written report can be withheld.
options.B: Decline, and issue the written report as the plan set out.
options.C: Agree to brief orally, filing the slides and speaking notes.
options.D: Pass the request to the chief audit executive for a decision.

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive decides how and to whom final engagement communications go; an oral one is allowed, but the auditor does not pick it.
questions.pre_read: Ask which stage this is, whether the requested form is ever allowed, and who decides the form of the final communication.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.3 has the chief audit executive settle, before issue, how final engagement communications are delivered and to whom. An oral final communication backed by slides or notes is possible, so the request is not improper in itself, but its form is not the auditor's to agree. Briefing orally and filing the notes, the closest choice, would be sound only once the chief audit executive had chosen that form.

wrong_explanations.A: Consulting legal counsel on releasing results and on legal protection is the chief audit executive's step (Standards 11.3, 5.2); the auditor passes the request on instead.
wrong_explanations.B: The Standards allow an oral final communication backed by slides or notes, and the chief audit executive, not the auditor, decides its form and sends it (Standards 11.3, 15.1).
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an oral briefing backed by filed slides and notes can be a valid final communication, but only the chief audit executive decides its form (Standard 11.3).

tips: Eliminate: A, because seeking legal advice on releasing results is the chief audit executive's step, and B, because the Standards allow oral final communications, so refusing is not the auditor's decision.
Final two: D beats C because an oral briefing may be acceptable, but Standard 11.3 gives the chief audit executive the decision on how final results are delivered.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor picks fitting methods during fieldwork, but the form and the recipients of the final communication are the chief audit executive's decision.
